subject: Random Effect Possible for Multi-Species Occupancy Model?

messages.author: 662574cc7a6f36c7
messages.subject: Random Effect Possible for Multi-Species Occupancy Model?
parts:
Hello,

I am attempting to create a single-season, multi-species occupancy model
for 3 species of freshwater turtles at the trap-level (where each of the
741 traps is treated as a "site" in the model) in "unmarked" to explore
potential interspecific competition in a resource-limited environment. Our
experimental design involves approximately 20 traps within each survey
location, so I want to include a random effect for our 34 survey locations
to account for this nested design, where the survey location is treated as
a factor. In the code below, our survey location is denoted by
"Site_number."

I am attempting to run this intercept-only model, assuming species
independence as a proof-of-concept before diving further into conditional
occupancy probabilities and species dependence.


*fit_1 <- occuMulti(detformulas = c('~1', '~1', '~1'),
stateformulas = c('~1 + (1|Site_number)', '~1 + (1|Site_number)', '~1 +
(1|Site_number)'), maxOrder = 1, data =
msom_data)*

This is the error that I receive:
*Error: This function does not support random effects*

Is there a better way to move forward with these models to incorporate a
random effect of our 34 survey locations?

I am attaching my very lengthy MSOM data to ensure the example is
reproducible. Thank you for your time and assistance!

All the best,
Emma

messages.subject: Re: Random Effect Possible for Multi-Species Occupancy Model?
parts:
Hi Emma,

Unfortunately unmarked doesn't support random effects for all models and
this is one that isn't currently supported. If you think it is important to
account for the nested design in the model (which seems like a good idea to
me), I think your only option at the moment is to fit the model in a
Bayesian framework which would allow you to specify the random effects. If
I recall correctly, Chris Rota's original paper on the model shared some
good Stan code that you could adapt. I've also included some JAGS code for
the model at the end of this email that you could use as a starting point.
I'm sure there are other papers that share better BUGS code as well.

Ken
-------

library(unmarked)
data(MesoCarnivores)

jags_data <- list(
y_coy = MesoCarnivores$coyote, #
coyote matrix
y_fox = MesoCarnivores$redfox, # red
fox matrix
N = nrow(MesoCarnivores$coyote), # num
sites
J = ncol(MesoCarnivores$coyote) # num
samples
)

cat(file="jags_multispecies_null.txt", "
model {

# State process
for (i in 1:N){
# latent occupancy state
Z[i] ~ dcat(Psi[1:4]) # Takes on values 1-4
}

# Occupancy probabilities / multinomial logit
Psi[1] <- exp(f1 + f2 + f12) # {11}
Psi[2] <- exp(f1) # {10}
Psi[3] <- exp(f2) # {01}
Psi[4] <- 1 # {00}

# Priors on natural parameters
f1 ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)
f2 ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)
f12 ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)

# Detection process
for (i in 1:N){

z1[i] <- (Z[i] == 1) + (Z[i] == 2) # is coyote present?
z2[i] <- (Z[i] == 1) + (Z[i] == 3) # is red fox present?

for (j in 1:J){
y_coy[i, j] ~ dbern(z1[i] * p1)
y_fox[i, j] ~ dbern(z2[i] * p2)
}
}

# Priors on p
p1 ~ dunif(0, 1)
p2 ~ dunif(0, 1)

}
")

library(jagsUI)

inits <- function(){
list(Z = rep(1, jags_data$N))
}

params <- c("f1", "f2", "f12", "p1", "p2")

fit <- jags(data = jags_data, inits = inits, parameters.to.save = params,
model.file = 'jags_multispecies_null.txt', n.chains = 3, n.iter

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Re: Random Effect Possible for Multi-Species Occupancy Model?
parts:
Hi, Ken!

Thank you so much for taking the time to reply and share your code. We'll
definitely consider using a Bayesian framework. I did have a follow-up
question regarding the process of fitting models using unmarked.

It is my understanding that one can fit models for species independently.
If I were to fit a model for two species, say A and B, could I perform
AIC-based model selection for detection for each species separately, use
those top models in modeling occupancy independently, and then take the top
four models (detection for A and B/occupancy for A and B) to perform model
selection for the species-interaction?

The workflow would look something like this:
~Species A det. vars. ~ 1 ~1 ~1 ~1 --> Model selection for species A det.
var. top model
~1 ~ Species B det. vars. ~1 ~1 ~1 --> Model selection for species B. det
var. top model
~Species A top. detection vars. ~ 1 ~Species A occ. vars. ~1 ~1 --> Model
selection for species A occ. var. top model
~1 ~ Species B top. detection vars. ~1 ~Species B. occ. vars. ~1 --> Model
selection for species B occ. var. top model

> Unfortunately unmarked doesn't support random effects for all models and
> this is one that isn't currently supported. If you think it is important to
> account for the nested design in the model (which seems like a good idea to
> me), I think your only option at the moment is to fit the model in a
> Bayesian framework which would allow you to specify the random effects. If
> I recall correctly, Chris Rota's original paper on the model shared some
> good Stan code that you could adapt. I've also included some JAGS code for
> the model at the end of this email that you could use as a starting point.
> I'm sure there are other papers that share better BUGS code as well.
>
> Ken
> -------
>
> library(unmarked)
> data(MesoCarnivores)
>
> jags_data <- list(
> y_coy = MesoCarnivores$coyote, #
> coyote matrix
> y_fox = MesoCarnivores$redfox, # red
> fox matrix
> N = nrow(MesoCarnivores$coyote), # num
> sites
> J = ncol(MesoCarnivores$coyote) # num
> samples
> )
>
> cat(file="jags_multispecies_null.txt", "
> model {
>
> # State process
> for (i in 1:N){
> # latent occupancy state
> Z[i] ~ dcat(Psi[1:4]) # Takes on values 1-4
> }
>
> # Occupancy probabilities / multinomial logit
> Psi[1] <- exp(f1 + f2 + f12) # {11}
> Psi[2] <- exp(f1) # {10}
> Psi[3] <- exp(f2) # {01}
> Psi[4] <- 1 # {00}
>
> # Priors on natural parameters
> f1 ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)
> f2 ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)
> f12 ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)
>
> # Detection process
> for (i in 1:N){
>
> z1[i] <- (Z[i] == 1) + (Z[i] == 2) # is coyote present?
> z2[i] <- (Z[i] == 1) + (Z[i] == 3) # is red fox present?
>
> for (j in 1:J){
> y_coy[i, j] ~ dbern(z1[i] * p1)
> y_fox[i, j] ~ dbern(z2[i] * p2)
> }
> }
>
> # Priors on p
> p1 ~ dunif(0, 1)
> p2 ~ dunif(0, 1)
>
> }
> ")
>
> library(jagsUI)
>
> inits <- function(){
> list(Z = rep(1, jags_data$N))
> }
>
> params <- c("f1", "f2", "f12", "p1", "p2")
>
> fit <- jags(data = jags_data, inits = inits, parameters.to.save = params,

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Re: Random Effect Possible for Multi-Species Occupancy Model?
parts:
Hi Emma,

You'll likely get different answers from different people on this question.
It also depends on if your main goal is inference/testing hypotheses, vs.
prediction.

In general, my preferred approach (for this and other model types) is to
think carefully about which covariates likely affect occupancy and
detection, and then fit a single model including those covariates. Or, if I
have a small set of well-defined alternative hypotheses, fit a model
corresponding to each hypothesis and then do model selection. I think in
most cases, taking a large pool of candidate covariates and feeding them
into a complicated, ad-hoc model selection workflow is rarely the best
approach.

Ken

On Sunday, September 7, 2025 at 8:03:10 PM UTC emwi...@ncsu.edu wrote:

> Hi, Ken!
>
> Thank you so much for taking the time to reply and share your code. We'll
> definitely consider using a Bayesian framework. I did have a follow-up
> question regarding the process of fitting models using unmarked.
>
> It is my understanding that one can fit models for species independently.
> If I were to fit a model for two species, say A and B, could I perform
> AIC-based model selection for detection for each species separately, use
> those top models in modeling occupancy independently, and then take the top
> four models (detection for A and B/occupancy for A and B) to perform model
> selection for the species-interaction?
>
> The workflow would look something like this:
> ~Species A det. vars. ~ 1 ~1 ~1 ~1 --> Model selection for species A det.
> var. top model
> ~1 ~ Species B det. vars. ~1 ~1 ~1 --> Model selection for species B. det
> var. top model
> ~Species A top. detection vars. ~ 1 ~Species A occ. vars. ~1 ~1 --> Model
> selection for species A occ. var. top model
> ~1 ~ Species B top. detection vars. ~1 ~Species B. occ. vars. ~1 --> Model
> selection for species B occ. var. top model
> ~Species A top. detection vars. ~ Species B top. detection vars. ~Species A
> top occ. vars ~Species B. top occ. vars. ~Interaction Vars. --> Model
> selection for interaction term top model
>
> Is this the recommended workflow, or are there certain steps that should be
> performed together/separated? Thank you so much for your time and
> assistance. Let me know if I can elaborate further.
>
> All the best,
> Emma
>
>
>
> On Mon, Sep 1, 2025 at 8:25 AM Ken Kellner <con...@kenkellner.com> wrote:
>
> > Hi Emma,
> >
> > Unfortunately unmarked doesn't support random effects for all models and
> > this is one that isn't currently supported. If you think it is important
> to
> > account for the nested design in the model (which seems like a good idea
> to
> > me), I think your only option at the moment is to fit the model in a
> > Bayesian framework which would allow you to specify the random effects.
> If
> > I recall correctly, Chris Rota's original paper on the model shared some
> > good Stan code that you could adapt. I've also included some JAGS code
> for
> > the model at the end of this email that you could use as a starting
> point.
> > I'm sure there are other papers that share better BUGS code as well.
> >
> > Ken
> > -------
> >
> > library(unmarked)
> > data(MesoCarnivores)
> >
> > jags_data <- list(
> > y_coy = MesoCarnivores$coyote, #
> > coyote matrix
> > y_fox = MesoCarnivores$redfox, # red
> > fox matrix
> > N = nrow(MesoCarnivores$coyote), # num
> > sites
> > J = ncol(MesoCarnivores$coyote) # num
> > samples
> > )
> >
> > cat(file="jags_multispecies_null.txt", "
> > model {
> >
> > # State process
> > for (i in 1:N){
> > # latent occupancy state
> > Z[i] ~ dcat(Psi[1:4]) # Takes on values 1-4
> > }
> >
> > # Occupancy probabilities / multinomial logit
> > Psi[1] <- exp(f1 + f2 + f12) # {11}
> > Psi[2] <- exp(f1) # {10}
> > Psi[3] <- exp(f2) # {01}
> > Psi[4] <- 1 # {00}
> >
> > # Priors on natural parameters
> > f1 ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)
> > f2 ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)
> > f12 ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)
> >
> > # Detection process
> > for (i in 1:N){
> >
> > z1[i] <- (Z[i] == 1) + (Z[i] == 2) # is coyote present?
> > z2[i] <- (Z[i] == 1) + (Z[i] == 3) # is red fox present?
> >
> > for (j in 1:J){
> > y_coy[i, j] ~ dbern(z1[i] * p1)
> > y_fox[i, j] ~ dbern(z2[i] * p2)
> > }
> > }
> >
> > # Priors on p
> > p1 ~ dunif(0, 1)
> > p2 ~ dunif(0, 1)
> >
> > }
> > ")
> >
> > library(jagsUI)
> >
> > inits <- function(){
> > list(Z = rep(1, jags_data$N))
> > }
> >
> > params <- c("f1", "f2", "f12", "p1", "p2")
> >
> > fit <- jags(data = jags_data, inits = inits, parameters.to.save = params,
> > model.file = 'jags_multispecies_null.txt', n.chains = 3,
> > n.iter = 1000,
> > n.burnin = 500, n.thin = 1, parallel = TRUE)
> >

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Re: Random Effect Possible for Multi-Species Occupancy Model?
parts:
Hi, Ken,

Thanks so much for your response! I had lost some sight of my original
question when model-building, but I have, I think, been able to get back on
track with hypothesis-testing. I was able to run model selection for three
models that look at the potential for interspecific interactions between
two species of turtles to see whether distance to permanent water sources,
urban cover in the landscape, day of year, and emergent vegetation
influence species interactions. The top model had only a slightly lower
AICc score compared to our null model of no interaction but was much higher
than our model that incorporated covariates, indicating that none of the
covariates included influence the species interactions.

I am in the process of performing a goodness of fit test for my top model
using the sum of squared Pearson residuals as a test statistic (e.g., Parsons
et al. 2018
<https://link-springer-com.prox.lib.ncsu.edu/article/10.1007/s13253-021-00482-y>).
I am attaching the top model used, as well as my code to calculate the test
statistic for both species and compare them to the simulated distributions
to assess model fit. My p-value for *Clemmys *indicates a relatively good
fit (=0.236), while the p-value for *Chrysemys* gives a value of 0, which
is concerning to me. Is this the recommended approach for evaluating model
fit, or is there another way that you would recommend? If there are any
pitfalls in my reasoning, please let me know. If the model isn't a good fit
for *Chrysemys*, I assume we'd also have to be suspicious of the
interaction term?

Thank you so much for your time and assistance!

All the best,
Emma

############## GOF TEST ##############
# Detection histories
ylist <- pairwise_dependence@data@ylist
clemmys_y <- ylist$clemmys # Observed data y (detections)
chrysemys_y <- ylist$chrysemys

# Predict detection probabilities for each species
p_clemmys <- predict(pairwise_dependence, type = "det", species =
"clemmys")$Predicted # p
p_chrysemys <- predict(pairwise_dependence, type = "det", species =
"chrysemys")$Predicted

# Reshape detection probabilities to 741 × 4 (sites × occasions)
p_clemmys_mat <- matrix(p_clemmys, nrow = 741, ncol = 4)
p_chrysemys_mat <- matrix(p_chrysemys, nrow = 741, ncol = 4)

# Predict occupancy probabilities for each species
psi_clemmys <- predict(pairwise_dependence, type = "state", species =
"clemmys")$Predicted # ψ
psi_chrysemys <- predict(pairwise_dependence, type = "state", species =
"chrysemys")$Predicted

# Repeat occupancy probabilities across 4 occasions for each site (741
sites)
psi_clemmys_mat <- matrix(rep(psi_clemmys, times = 4), nrow = 741, ncol = 4)
psi_chrysemys_mat <- matrix(rep(psi_chrysemys, times = 4), nrow = 741, ncol
= 4)

#
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Calculate expected detection probabilities μ = E(Y) = ψ × p
#
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
mu_clemmys <- psi_clemmys_mat * p_clemmys_mat # μ for Clemmys
mu_chrysemys <- psi_chrysemys_mat * p_chrysemys_mat # μ for Chrysemys

#
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Calculate squared Pearson residuals r_P^2 = (y - μ)^2 / V(μ)
# y = observed detection/non-detection (clemmys_y, chrysemys_y)
# μ = expected detection probability = ψ p (mu_*)
# V(μ) = μ (1 - μ)
#
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
r2_clemmys <- (clemmys_y - mu_clemmys)^2 / (mu_clemmys * (1 - mu_clemmys))
r2_chrysemys <- (chrysemys_y - mu_chrysemys)^2 / (mu_chrysemys * (1 -
mu_chrysemys))

#
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Sum squared Pearson residuals across all sites and occasions to get test
statistics
#
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
T_clemmys <- sum(r2_clemmys, na.rm = TRUE)
T_chrysemys <- sum(r2_chrysemys, na.rm = TRUE)

#
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Simulation to evaluate model fit
#
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
n_sim <- 1000
set.seed(123) # for reproducibility

T_rep_clemmys <- numeric(n_sim)
T_rep_chrysemys <- numeric(n_sim)

for (s in 1:n_sim) {
# Simulate latent occupancy state z ~ Bernoulli(ψ)
z_clemmys <- rbinom(741, 1, psi_clemmys)
z_chrysemys <- rbinom(741, 1, psi_chrysemys)

# Expand z to site × occasion matrices (repeat times=4)
z_clemmys_mat <- matrix(rep(z_clemmys, times = 4), nrow = 741, ncol = 4)
z_chrysemys_mat <- matrix(rep(z_chrysemys, times = 4), nrow = 741, ncol =
4)

# Calculate detection probabilities conditional on occupancy: P(y=1|z) =
z × p
prob_clemmys <- z_clemmys_mat * p_clemmys_mat
prob_chrysemys <- z_chrysemys_mat * p_chrysemys_mat

# Simulate detection/non-detection observations y ~ Bernoulli(z p)
y_rep_clemmys <- matrix(rbinom(length(prob_clemmys), 1,
as.vector(prob_clemmys)), nrow = 741)
y_rep_chrysemys <- matrix(rbinom(length(prob_chrysemys), 1,
as.vector(prob_chrysemys)), nrow = 741)

# Calculate squared Pearson residuals for simulated data, same formula as
above
r2_rep_clemmys <- (y_rep_clemmys - mu_clemmys)^2 / (mu_clemmys * (1 -
mu_clemmys))
r2_rep_chrysemys <- (y_rep_chrysemys - mu_chrysemys)^2 / (mu_chrysemys *
(1 - mu_chrysemys))

# Sum squared residuals to get test statistic for this simulation
T_rep_clemmys[s] <- sum(r2_rep_clemmys, na.rm = TRUE)
T_rep_chrysemys[s] <- sum(r2_rep_chrysemys, na.rm = TRUE)
}

# Calculate p-values
p_clemmys <- mean(T_rep_clemmys >= T_clemmys)
p_chrysemys <- mean(T_rep_chrysemys >= T_chrysemys)

On Mon, Sep 8, 2025 at 12:31 PM Ken Kellner <con...@kenkellner.com> wrote:

> Hi Emma,
>
> You'll likely get different answers from different people on this
> question. It also depends on if your main goal is inference/testing
> hypotheses, vs. prediction.
>
> In general, my preferred approach (for this and other model types) is to
> think carefully about which covariates likely affect occupancy and
> detection, and then fit a single model including those covariates. Or, if I
> have a small set of well-defined alternative hypotheses, fit a model
> corresponding to each hypothesis and then do model selection. I think in
> most cases, taking a large pool of candidate covariates and feeding them
> into a complicated, ad-hoc model selection workflow is rarely the best
> approach.
>
> Ken
>
> On Sunday, September 7, 2025 at 8:03:10 PM UTC emwi...@ncsu.edu wrote:

>> Hi, Ken!
>>
>> Thank you so much for taking the time to reply and share your code. We'll
>> definitely consider using a Bayesian framework. I did have a follow-up
>> question regarding the process of fitting models using unmarked.
>>
>> It is my understanding that one can fit models for species independently.
>> If I were to fit a model for two species, say A and B, could I perform
>> AIC-based model selection for detection for each species separately, use
>> those top models in modeling occupancy independently, and then take the
>> top
>> four models (detection for A and B/occupancy for A and B) to perform
>> model
>> selection for the species-interaction?
>>
>> The workflow would look something like this:
>> ~Species A det. vars. ~ 1 ~1 ~1 ~1 --> Model selection for species A det.
>> var. top model
>> ~1 ~ Species B det. vars. ~1 ~1 ~1 --> Model selection for species B. det
>> var. top model
>> ~Species A top. detection vars. ~ 1 ~Species A occ. vars. ~1 ~1 --> Model
>> selection for species A occ. var. top model
>> ~1 ~ Species B top. detection vars. ~1 ~Species B. occ. vars. ~1 -->
>> Model
>> selection for species B occ. var. top model
>> ~Species A top. detection vars. ~ Species B top. detection vars. ~Species
>> A
>> top occ. vars ~Species B. top occ. vars. ~Interaction Vars. --> Model
>> selection for interaction term top model
>>
>> Is this the recommended workflow, or are there certain steps that should
>> be
>> performed together/separated? Thank you so much for your time and
>> assistance. Let me know if I can elaborate further.
>>
>> All the best,
>> Emma
>>
>>
>>
>> On Mon, Sep 1, 2025 at 8:25 AM Ken Kellner <con...@kenkellner.com>
>> wrote:

>> > Hi Emma,

>> > }
>> > ")

statistic. I think that's a reasonable approach to use for this model.
Unfortunately there isn't one specific goodness-of-fit test that's
recommended for the multispecies model, but I have seen this approach used
before.

unmarked has tools to make this process easier which you might want to try,
specifically the parboot() function. See example code below (which I have
not tested on your data but should work).

Ken

# Calculate sum of squared pearson residuals from a fitted model
pearson2 <- function(fit){ # only argument is the fitted model object
y <- fit@data@ylist
S <- length(y) # number of species
yhat <- fitted(fit)

out <- lapply(1:S, function(s){
(y[[s]] - yhat[[s]])^2 / (yhat[[s]] * (1-yhat[[s]]))
})

sum(unlist(out)) # sum them up across all species
}

# Run a parametric bootstrap
# 30 simulations (should use more)
pb <- parboot(pairwise_dependence, statistic = pearson2, nsim = 30)
pb
plot(pb)

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Re: Random Effect Possible for Multi-Species Occupancy Model?
parts:
Hi, Ken!

Thanks so much for providing this script. It looks like I was trying to
reinvent the wheel! The script worked well and provided the following
output.

Call: parboot(object = pairwise_dependence, statistic = pearson2, nsim =
1000)

Parametric Bootstrap Statistics:
t0 mean(t0 - t_B) StdDev(t0 - t_B) Pr(t_B > t0)
1 5206 -365 931 0.696

t_B quantiles:
0% 2.5% 25% 50% 75% 97.5% 100%
[1,] 4020 4565 5136 5415 5719 7616 20413

t0 = Original statistic computed from data
t_B = Vector of bootstrap samples

If I am understanding it correctly, it looks like there is not any evidence
of lack of fit. Does the model need to be evaluated for each species
separately, or is summing across species recommended instead (as above)?

Thanks for your time and feedback!

All the best,
Emma

On Fri, Sep 12, 2025 at 12:17 PM Ken Kellner <con...@kenkellner.com> wrote:

> Hi Emma,
>
> It's a bit hard to parse the code but it looks like you're doing a
> parametric bootstrap with a sum of squared Pearson residuals test
> statistic. I think that's a reasonable approach to use for this model.
> Unfortunately there isn't one specific goodness-of-fit test that's
> recommended for the multispecies model, but I have seen this approach used
> before.
>
> unmarked has tools to make this process easier which you might want to
> try, specifically the parboot() function. See example code below (which I
> have not tested on your data but should work).
>
> Ken
>
> # Calculate sum of squared pearson residuals from a fitted model
> pearson2 <- function(fit){ # only argument is the fitted model object
> y <- fit@data@ylist
> S <- length(y) # number of species
> yhat <- fitted(fit)
>
> out <- lapply(1:S, function(s){
> (y[[s]] - yhat[[s]])^2 / (yhat[[s]] * (1-yhat[[s]]))
> })
>
> sum(unlist(out)) # sum them up across all species
> }
>
> # Run a parametric bootstrap
> # 30 simulations (should use more)
> pb <- parboot(pairwise_dependence, statistic = pearson2, nsim = 30)
> pb
> plot(pb)
>
> On Thursday, September 11, 2025 at 8:35:13 PM UTC emwi...@ncsu.edu wrote:
>
>> Hi, Ken,
>>
>> Thanks so much for your response! I had lost some sight of my original
>> question when model-building, but I have, I think, been able to get back
>> on
>> track with hypothesis-testing. I was able to run model selection for
>> three
>> models that look at the potential for interspecific interactions between
>> two species of turtles to see whether distance to permanent water
>> sources,
>> urban cover in the landscape, day of year, and emergent vegetation
>> influence species interactions. The top model had only a slightly lower
>> AICc score compared to our null model of no interaction but was much
>> higher
>> than our model that incorporated covariates, indicating that none of the
>> covariates included influence the species interactions.
>>
>> I am in the process of performing a goodness of fit test for my top model
>> using the sum of squared Pearson residuals as a test statistic (e.g.,
>> Parsons
>> et al. 2018
>> <
>> https://link-springer-com.prox.lib.ncsu.edu/article/10.1007/s13253-021-00482-y>).
>>
>> I am attaching the top model used, as well as my code to calculate the
>> test
>> statistic for both species and compare them to the simulated
>> distributions
>> to assess model fit. My p-value for *Clemmys *indicates a relatively good
>> fit (=0.236), while the p-value for *Chrysemys* gives a value of 0, which
>> is concerning to me. Is this the recommended approach for evaluating
>> model
>> fit, or is there another way that you would recommend? If there are any
>> pitfalls in my reasoning, please let me know. If the model isn't a good
>> fit
>> for *Chrysemys*, I assume we'd also have to be suspicious of the
>> interaction term?
>>
>> Thank you so much for your time and assistance!
>>
>> All the best,
>> Emma
>>
>> ############## GOF TEST ##############
>> # Detection histories
>> ylist <- pairwise_dependence@data@ylist
>> clemmys_y <- ylist$clemmys # Observed data y (detections)
>> chrysemys_y <- ylist$chrysemys
>>
>> # Predict detection probabilities for each species
>> p_clemmys <- predict(pairwise_dependence, type = "det", species =
>> "clemmys")$Predicted # p
>> p_chrysemys <- predict(pairwise_dependence, type = "det", species =
>> "chrysemys")$Predicted
>>
>> # Reshape detection probabilities to 741 × 4 (sites × occasions)
>> p_clemmys_mat <- matrix(p_clemmys, nrow = 741, ncol = 4)
>> p_chrysemys_mat <- matrix(p_chrysemys, nrow = 741, ncol = 4)
>>
>> # Predict occupancy probabilities for each species
>> psi_clemmys <- predict(pairwise_dependence, type = "state", species =
>> "clemmys")$Predicted # ψ
>> psi_chrysemys <- predict(pairwise_dependence, type = "state", species =
>> "chrysemys")$Predicted
>>
>> # Repeat occupancy probabilities across 4 occasions for each site (741
>> sites)
>> psi_clemmys_mat <- matrix(rep(psi_clemmys, times = 4), nrow = 741, ncol =
>> 4)
>> psi_chrysemys_mat <- matrix(rep(psi_chrysemys, times = 4), nrow = 741,
>> ncol
>> = 4)
>>
>> #
>> -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
>>
>> # Calculate expected detection probabilities μ = E(Y) = ψ × p
>> #
>> -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
>>
>> mu_clemmys <- psi_clemmys_mat * p_clemmys_mat # μ for Clemmys
>> mu_chrysemys <- psi_chrysemys_mat * p_chrysemys_mat # μ for Chrysemys
>>
>> #
>> -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
>>
>> # Calculate squared Pearson residuals r_P^2 = (y - μ)^2 / V(μ)
>> # y = observed detection/non-detection (clemmys_y, chrysemys_y)
>> # μ = expected detection probability = ψ p (mu_*)
>> # V(μ) = μ (1 - μ)
>> #
>> -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
>>
>> r2_clemmys <- (clemmys_y - mu_clemmys)^2 / (mu_clemmys * (1 -
>> mu_clemmys))
>> r2_chrysemys <- (chrysemys_y - mu_chrysemys)^2 / (mu_chrysemys * (1 -
>> mu_chrysemys))
>>
>> #
>> -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
>>
>> # Sum squared Pearson residuals across all sites and occasions to get
>> test
>> statistics
>> #
>> -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
>>
>> T_clemmys <- sum(r2_clemmys, na.rm = TRUE)
>> T_chrysemys <- sum(r2_chrysemys, na.rm = TRUE)
>>
>> #
>> -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
>>
>> # Simulation to evaluate model fit
>> #
>> -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
>>
>> n_sim <- 1000
>> set.seed(123) # for reproducibility
>>
>> T_rep_clemmys <- numeric(n_sim)

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Re: Random Effect Possible for Multi-Species Occupancy Model?
parts:
Hi Emma,

Yes, that's how I'd interpret it. I think you could make a case for either
looking at species separately or pooling them, it might be interesting to
do both. You'd have to modify the pearson2 function to look at individual
species.

Ken

On Saturday, September 13, 2025 at 12:22:03 AM UTC emwi...@ncsu.edu wrote:

> Hi, Ken!
>
> Thanks so much for providing this script. It looks like I was trying to
> reinvent the wheel! The script worked well and provided the following
> output.
>
> Call: parboot(object = pairwise_dependence, statistic = pearson2, nsim =
> 1000)
>
> Parametric Bootstrap Statistics:
> t0 mean(t0 - t_B) StdDev(t0 - t_B) Pr(t_B > t0)
> 1 5206 -365 931 0.696
>
> t_B quantiles:
> 0% 2.5% 25% 50% 75% 97.5% 100%
> [1,] 4020 4565 5136 5415 5719 7616 20413
>
> t0 = Original statistic computed from data
> t_B = Vector of bootstrap samples
>
> If I am understanding it correctly, it looks like there is not any evidence
> of lack of fit. Does the model need to be evaluated for each species
> separately, or is summing across species recommended instead (as above)?
>
> Thanks for your time and feedback!
>
> All the best,
> Emma
>
> On Fri, Sep 12, 2025 at 12:17 PM Ken Kellner <con...@kenkellner.com>
> wrote:
>
> > Hi Emma,
> >
> > It's a bit hard to parse the code but it looks like you're doing a
> > parametric bootstrap with a sum of squared Pearson residuals test
> > statistic. I think that's a reasonable approach to use for this model.
> > Unfortunately there isn't one specific goodness-of-fit test that's
> > recommended for the multispecies model, but I have seen this approach
> used
> > before.
> >
> > unmarked has tools to make this process easier which you might want to
> > try, specifically the parboot() function. See example code below (which I
> > have not tested on your data but should work).
> >
> > Ken
> >
> > # Calculate sum of squared pearson residuals from a fitted model
> > pearson2 <- function(fit){ # only argument is the fitted model object
> > y <- fit@data@ylist
> > S <- length(y) # number of species
> > yhat <- fitted(fit)
> >
> > out <- lapply(1:S, function(s){
> > (y[[s]] - yhat[[s]])^2 / (yhat[[s]] * (1-yhat[[s]]))
> > })
> >
> > sum(unlist(out)) # sum them up across all species
> > }
> >
> > # Run a parametric bootstrap
> > # 30 simulations (should use more)
> > pb <- parboot(pairwise_dependence, statistic = pearson2, nsim = 30)
> > pb
> > plot(pb)
> >
> > On Thursday, September 11, 2025 at 8:35:13 PM UTC emwi...@ncsu.edu
> wrote:
> >
> >> Hi, Ken,
> >>
> >> Thanks so much for your response! I had lost some sight of my original
> >> question when model-building, but I have, I think, been able to get back
> >> on
> >> track with hypothesis-testing. I was able to run model selection for
> >> three
> >> models that look at the potential for interspecific interactions between
> >> two species of turtles to see whether distance to permanent water
> >> sources,
> >> urban cover in the landscape, day of year, and emergent vegetation
> >> influence species interactions. The top model had only a slightly lower
> >> AICc score compared to our null model of no interaction but was much
> >> higher
> >> than our model that incorporated covariates, indicating that none of the
> >> covariates included influence the species interactions.
> >>
> >> I am in the process of performing a goodness of fit test for my top
> model
> >> using the sum of squared Pearson residuals as a test statistic (e.g.,
> >> Parsons
> >> et al. 2018
> >> <
> >>
> https://link-springer-com.prox.lib.ncsu.edu/article/10.1007/s13253-021-00482-y
> >).
> >>
> >> I am attaching the top model used, as well as my code to calculate the
> >> test
> >> statistic for both species and compare them to the simulated
> >> distributions
> >> to assess model fit. My p-value for *Clemmys *indicates a relatively
> good
> >> fit (=0.236), while the p-value for *Chrysemys* gives a value of 0,
> which
> >> is concerning to me. Is this the recommended approach for evaluating
> >> model
> >> fit, or is there another way that you would recommend? If there are any
> >> pitfalls in my reasoning, please let me know. If the model isn't a good
> >> fit
> >> for *Chrysemys*, I assume we'd also have to be suspicious of the
> >> interaction term?
> >>
> >> Thank you so much for your time and assistance!
> >>
> >> All the best,
> >> Emma
> >>
> >> ############## GOF TEST ##############
> >> # Detection histories
> >> ylist <- pairwise_dependence@data@ylist
> >> clemmys_y <- ylist$clemmys # Observed data y (detections)
> >> chrysemys_y <- ylist$chrysemys
> >>
> >> # Predict detection probabilities for each species
> >> p_clemmys <- predict(pairwise_dependence, type = "det", species =
> >> "clemmys")$Predicted # p
> >> p_chrysemys <- predict(pairwise_dependence, type = "det", species =
> >> "chrysemys")$Predicted
> >>
> >> # Reshape detection probabilities to 741 × 4 (sites × occasions)
> >> p_clemmys_mat <- matrix(p_clemmys, nrow = 741, ncol = 4)
> >> p_chrysemys_mat <- matrix(p_chrysemys, nrow = 741, ncol = 4)
> >>
> >> # Predict occupancy probabilities for each species
> >> psi_clemmys <- predict(pairwise_dependence, type = "state", species =
> >> "clemmys")$Predicted # ψ
> >> psi_chrysemys <- predict(pairwise_dependence, type = "state", species =
> >> "chrysemys")$Predicted
> >>
> >> # Repeat occupancy probabilities across 4 occasions for each site (741
> >> sites)
> >> psi_clemmys_mat <- matrix(rep(psi_clemmys, times = 4), nrow = 741, ncol
> =
> >> 4)
> >> psi_chrysemys_mat <- matrix(rep(psi_chrysemys, times = 4), nrow = 741,
> >> ncol
> >> = 4)
> >>
> >> #
> >>
> -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
> >>
> >> # Calculate expected detection probabilities μ = E(Y) = ψ × p
> >> #
> >>
> -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
> >>
> >> mu_clemmys <- psi_clemmys_mat * p_clemmys_mat # μ for Clemmys
> >> mu_chrysemys <- psi_chrysemys_mat * p_chrysemys_mat # μ for Chrysemys
> >>
> >> #
> >>
> -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
> >>
> >> # Calculate squared Pearson residuals r_P^2 = (y - μ)^2 / V(μ)
> >> # y = observed detection/non-detection (clemmys_y, chrysemys_y)
> >> # μ = expected detection probability = ψ p (mu_*)
> >> # V(μ) = μ (1 - μ)
> >> #
> >>
> -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
> >>
> >> r2_clemmys <- (clemmys_y - mu_clemmys)^2 / (mu_clemmys * (1 -
> >> mu_clemmys))
> >> r2_chrysemys <- (chrysemys_y - mu_chrysemys)^2 / (mu_chrysemys * (1 -
> >> mu_chrysemys))
> >>
> >> #
> >>
> -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
> >>
> >> # Sum squared Pearson residuals across all sites and occasions to get
> >> test
> >> statistics
> >> #
> >>
> -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
> >>
> >> T_clemmys <- sum(r2_clemmys, na.rm = TRUE)
> >> T_chrysemys <- sum(r2_chrysemys, na.rm = TRUE)
> >>
> >> #
> >>
> -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
> >>
> >> # Simulation to evaluate model fit
> >> #
> >>
> -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
> >>
> >> n_sim <- 1000
> >> set.seed(123) # for reproducibility
> >>
> >> T_rep_clemmys <- numeric(n_sim)
> >> T_rep_chrysemys <- numeric(n_sim)
> >>
> >> for (s in 1:n_sim) {
> >> # Simulate latent occupancy state z ~ Bernoulli(ψ)
> >> z_clemmys <- rbinom(741, 1, psi_clemmys)
> >> z_chrysemys <- rbinom(741, 1, psi_chrysemys)
> >>
> >> # Expand z to site × occasion matrices (repeat times=4)
> >> z_clemmys_mat <- matrix(rep(z_clemmys, times = 4), nrow = 741, ncol = 4)
> >> z_chrysemys_mat <- matrix(rep(z_chrysemys, times = 4), nrow = 741, ncol
> =
> >> 4)
> >>
> >> # Calculate detection probabilities conditional on occupancy: P(y=1|z) =
> >> z × p
> >> prob_clemmys <- z_clemmys_mat * p_clemmys_mat
> >> prob_chrysemys <- z_chrysemys_mat * p_chrysemys_mat
> >>
> >> # Simulate detection/non-detection observations y ~ Bernoulli(z p)
> >> y_rep_clemmys <- matrix(rbinom(length(prob_clemmys), 1,
> >> as.vector(prob_clemmys)), nrow = 741)
> >> y_rep_chrysemys <- matrix(rbinom(length(prob_chrysemys), 1,
> >> as.vector(prob_chrysemys)), nrow = 741)
> >>
> >> # Calculate squared Pearson residuals for simulated data, same formula
> as
> >> above
> >> r2_rep_clemmys <- (y_rep_clemmys - mu_clemmys)^2 / (mu_clemmys * (1 -
> >> mu_clemmys))
> >> r2_rep_chrysemys <- (y_rep_chrysemys - mu_chrysemys)^2 / (mu_chrysemys *
> >> (1 - mu_chrysemys))
> >>
> >> # Sum squared residuals to get test statistic for this simulation
> >> T_rep_clemmys[s] <- sum(r2_rep_clemmys, na.rm = TRUE)
> >> T_rep_chrysemys[s] <- sum(r2_rep_chrysemys, na.rm = TRUE)
> >> }
> >>
> >> # Calculate p-values
> >> p_clemmys <- mean(T_rep_clemmys >= T_clemmys)
> >> p_chrysemys <- mean(T_rep_chrysemys >= T_chrysemys)
> >>
> >>
> >>
> >> On Mon, Sep 8, 2025 at 12:31 PM Ken Kellner <con...@kenkellner.com>
> >> wrote:
> >>
> >> > Hi Emma,
> >> >
> >> > You'll likely get different answers from different people on this
> >> > question. It also depends on if your main goal is inference/testing
> >> > hypotheses, vs. prediction.
> >> >
> >> > In general, my preferred approach (for this and other model types) is
> >> to
> >> > think carefully about which covariates likely affect occupancy and
> >> > detection, and then fit a single model including those covariates. Or,
> >> if I
> >> > have a small set of well-defined alternative hypotheses, fit a model

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Re: Random Effect Possible for Multi-Species Occupancy Model?
parts:
Hi, Ken!

Thanks for your response. Glad to hear everything is on the right track.
When using k-fold cross-validation for model selection (two models without
penalty and one model fitted with penalized likelihood), does the
crossVal() function in unmarked() apply some penalty similar to AIC that
ensures the top model selected is not always the most parameterized?

I've attached the code that I am using for reference. I pulled it from
another discussion in this Google Group. Thanks again!

All the best,
Emma

# Run first part of ?occuMulti example to get fitted model
fit <- independence_mod
fit2 <- pairwise_dependence
fit3 <- mediated_conditional

set.seed(123)

# Find best value of penalty for a single model and re-fit the model with
that penalty
# Uses k-fold cross validation
# fit_opt <- optimizePenalty(fit, penalties=c(0,1,2))

# Compare models

# Function to extract cross-validation score for each penalty
get_crossval <- function(object, penalties, k=5){
folds <- unmarked:::partitionKfold(object, k)

cvp <- sapply(penalties, function(p, k, fit, folds){
cv <- sapply(1:k, function(i){
refit <- update(fit, data=folds[[i]]$trainData, penalty=p, se=FALSE)
sum(unmarked:::occuMultiLogLik(refit, folds[[i]]$testData))
})
sum(cv)
}, k=k, fit=object, folds=folds)
data.frame(model=deparse(substitute(object)), penalty=penalties,
value=cvp)
}

# Get CV scores for a range of penalty values for each model
fit_scores <- get_crossval(fit, penalties=c(2 ^ seq(-5, 5)), k=5)
fit2_scores <- get_crossval(fit2, penalties=c(2 ^ seq(-5, 5)), k=5)
fit3_scores <- get_crossval(fit3, penalties=c(2 ^ seq(-5, 5)), k=5)

# Combine and sort. Max CV value = top model
results <- rbind(fit_scores, fit2_scores, fit3_scores)
results[rev(order(results$value)),]

>> > Hi Emma,
>> >
>> > It's a bit hard to parse the code but it looks like you're doing a
>> > parametric bootstrap with a sum of squared Pearson residuals test
>> > statistic. I think that's a reasonable approach to use for this model.
>> > Unfortunately there isn't one specific goodness-of-fit test that's
>> > recommended for the multispecies model, but I have seen this approach
>> used
>> > before.
>> >
>> > unmarked has tools to make this process easier which you might want to
>> > try, specifically the parboot() function. See example code below (which
>> I
>> > have not tested on your data but should work).
>> >
>> > Ken
>> >
>> > # Calculate sum of squared pearson residuals from a fitted model
>> > pearson2 <- function(fit){ # only argument is the fitted model object
>> > y <- fit@data@ylist
>> > S <- length(y) # number of species
>> > yhat <- fitted(fit)
>> >
>> > out <- lapply(1:S, function(s){
>> > (y[[s]] - yhat[[s]])^2 / (yhat[[s]] * (1-yhat[[s]]))
>> > })
>> >
>> > sum(unlist(out)) # sum them up across all species
>> > }
>> >
>> > # Run a parametric bootstrap
>> > # 30 simulations (should use more)
>> > pb <- parboot(pairwise_dependence, statistic = pearson2, nsim = 30)
>> > pb
>> > plot(pb)
>> >
>> > On Thursday, September 11, 2025 at 8:35:13 PM UTC emwi...@ncsu.edu
>> wrote:
>> >
>> >> Hi, Ken,
>> >>
>> >> Thanks so much for your response! I had lost some sight of my original
>> >> question when model-building, but I have, I think, been able to get
>> back
>> >> on
>> >> track with hypothesis-testing. I was able to run model selection for
>> >> three
>> >> models that look at the potential for interspecific interactions
>> between
>> >> two species of turtles to see whether distance to permanent water
>> >> sources,
>> >> urban cover in the landscape, day of year, and emergent vegetation
>> >> influence species interactions. The top model had only a slightly
>> lower
>> >> AICc score compared to our null model of no interaction but was much
>> >> higher
>> >> than our model that incorporated covariates, indicating that none of
>> the
>> >> covariates included influence the species interactions.
>> >>
>> >> I am in the process of performing a goodness of fit test for my top
>> model
>> >> using the sum of squared Pearson residuals as a test statistic (e.g.,
>> >> Parsons
>> >> et al. 2018
>> >> <
>> >>
>> https://link-springer-com.prox.lib.ncsu.edu/article/10.1007/s13253-021-00482-y>).
>>
>> >>
>> >> I am attaching the top model used, as well as my code to calculate the
>> >> test
>> >> statistic for both species and compare them to the simulated
>> >> distributions
>> >> to assess model fit. My p-value for *Clemmys *indicates a relatively
>> good
>> >> fit (=0.236), while the p-value for *Chrysemys* gives a value of 0,
>> which
>> >> is concerning to me. Is this the recommended approach for evaluating
>> >> model
>> >> fit, or is there another way that you would recommend? If there are
>> any
>> >> pitfalls in my reasoning, please let me know. If the model isn't a
>> good
>> >> fit
>> >> for *Chrysemys*, I assume we'd also have to be suspicious of the
>> >> interaction term?
>> >>
>> >> Thank you so much for your time and assistance!
>> >>
>> >> All the best,
>> >> Emma
>> >>
>> >> ############## GOF TEST ##############
>> >> # Detection histories
>> >> ylist <- pairwise_dependence@data@ylist
>> >> clemmys_y <- ylist$clemmys # Observed data y (detections)
>> >> chrysemys_y <- ylist$chrysemys
>> >>
>> >> # Predict detection probabilities for each species
>> >> p_clemmys <- predict(pairwise_dependence, type = "det", species =
>> >> "clemmys")$Predicted # p
>> >> p_chrysemys <- predict(pairwise_dependence, type = "det", species =
>> >> "chrysemys")$Predicted
>> >>
>> >> # Reshape detection probabilities to 741 × 4 (sites × occasions)
>> >> p_clemmys_mat <- matrix(p_clemmys, nrow = 741, ncol = 4)
>> >> p_chrysemys_mat <- matrix(p_chrysemys, nrow = 741, ncol = 4)
>> >>
>> >> # Predict occupancy probabilities for each species
>> >> psi_clemmys <- predict(pairwise_dependence, type = "state", species =
>> >> "clemmys")$Predicted # ψ
>> >> psi_chrysemys <- predict(pairwise_dependence, type = "state", species
>> =
>> >> "chrysemys")$Predicted
>> >>
>> >> # Repeat occupancy probabilities across 4 occasions for each site (741
>> >> sites)
>> >> psi_clemmys_mat <- matrix(rep(psi_clemmys, times = 4), nrow = 741,
>> ncol =
>> >> 4)
>> >> psi_chrysemys_mat <- matrix(rep(psi_chrysemys, times = 4), nrow = 741,
>> >> ncol
>> >> = 4)
>> >>
>> >> #
>> >>
>> -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
>>
>> >>
>> >> # Calculate expected detection probabilities μ = E(Y) = ψ × p
>> >> #
>> >>
>> -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
>>
>> >>
>> >> mu_clemmys <- psi_clemmys_mat * p_clemmys_mat # μ for Clemmys
>> >> mu_chrysemys <- psi_chrysemys_mat * p_chrysemys_mat # μ for Chrysemys
>> >>
>> >> #
>> >>
>> -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
>>
>> >>
>> >> # Calculate squared Pearson residuals r_P^2 = (y - μ)^2 / V(μ)
>> >> # y = observed detection/non-detection (clemmys_y, chrysemys_y)
>> >> # μ = expected detection probability = ψ p (mu_*)
>> >> # V(μ) = μ (1 - μ)
>> >> #
>> >>
>> -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
>>
>> >>
>> >> r2_clemmys <- (clemmys_y - mu_clemmys)^2 / (mu_clemmys * (1 -
>> >> mu_clemmys))
>> >> r2_chrysemys <- (chrysemys_y - mu_chrysemys)^2 / (mu_chrysemys * (1 -
>> >> mu_chrysemys))
>> >>
>> >> #
>> >>
>> -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
>>
>> >>
>> >> # Sum squared Pearson residuals across all sites and occasions to get
>> >> test
>> >> statistics
>> >> #
>> >>
>> -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
>>
>> >>
>> >> T_clemmys <- sum(r2_clemmys, na.rm = TRUE)
>> >> T_chrysemys <- sum(r2_chrysemys, na.rm = TRUE)
>> >>
>> >> #
>> >>
>> -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
>>
>> >>
>> >> # Simulation to evaluate model fit
>> >> #
>> >>
>> -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
>>
>> >>
>> >> n_sim <- 1000
>> >> set.seed(123) # for reproducibility
>> >>
>> >> T_rep_clemmys <- numeric(n_sim)
>> >> T_rep_chrysemys <- numeric(n_sim)
>> >>
>> >> for (s in 1:n_sim) {
>> >> # Simulate latent occupancy state z ~ Bernoulli(ψ)
>> >> z_clemmys <- rbinom(741, 1, psi_clemmys)
>> >> z_chrysemys <- rbinom(741, 1, psi_chrysemys)
>> >>
>> >> # Expand z to site × occasion matrices (repeat times=4)
>> >> z_clemmys_mat <- matrix(rep(z_clemmys, times = 4), nrow = 741, ncol =
>> 4)
>> >> z_chrysemys_mat <- matrix(rep(z_chrysemys, times = 4), nrow = 741,
>> ncol =
>> >> 4)
>> >>
>> >> # Calculate detection probabilities conditional on occupancy: P(y=1|z)
>> =
>> >> z × p
>> >> prob_clemmys <- z_clemmys_mat * p_clemmys_mat
>> >> prob_chrysemys <- z_chrysemys_mat * p_chrysemys_mat
